claims.text: MCP defines a JSON-RPC `ping` method that either side may invoke; the receiver MUST return an empty result promptly, and timeout MAY be treated as connection failure.
MCP `ping` is the only spec-canonical health primitive that works uniformly across stdio and HTTP transports.
The MCP spec calls ping "optional," and most SDKs auto-implement the responder side but the client must initiate.
Ping checks the JSON-RPC layer but not downstream dependencies such as DB or upstream API.
HTTP MCP servers typically expose `/health` and `/ready` endpoints for liveness versus readiness, but stdio MCP servers have no HTTP surface.
The recommended substitute for HTTP `/health` on stdio MCP servers is periodic JSON-RPC `ping`, with a 30-second interval and a 2–5-second timeout.
Fast.io recommends three consecutive failed ping checks before triggering a restart of an MCP server.

A successful MCP ping confirms the message loop is unblocked and JSON-RPC serialization works, but does not confirm the server can answer tool calls dependent on downstream DB, auth, or file-system access.
Production-leaning patterns add an "internal health-check tool" callable by the operator/client to assert downstream dependencies of an MCP server.
None of this project's seven MCP servers have been verified to expose an internal health-check tool.
Claude Code automatically reconnects HTTP and SSE MCP servers that disconnect mid-session, with up to five attempts and exponential backoff starting at one second.
claims.notes: F2.1; cites Anthropic Claude Code MCP docs.

claims.text: Stdio MCP servers are local processes and are not reconnected automatically by Claude Code; when a stdio process dies, the server is marked failed and only operator action recovers it.
claims.notes: F2.1; verbatim spec quote inside paraphrase.

claims.text: As of Claude Code v2.1.121, initial-connect failures (5xx, connection refused, timeout) on HTTP/SSE retry up to three times.

Six of the seven MCP servers in this feature (Serena, mcp-openapi-schema, actionlint-mcp, Terraform MCP, GitNexus, codebase-memory-mcp) are most naturally stdio; only Context7 and Exa have remote-HTTP variants.
The `/mcp` slash-command in-session shows per-server state (connected / pending / failed) and tool count.
`claude mcp list` at the shell shows configured servers and their connection status.
A reconnecting Claude Code MCP server shows `pending`; after five failed reconnects it shows `failed` and is retried only on operator action.
Claude Code v2.1.62 had a known bug where `claude mcp list` returned empty output (GitHub issue #29492), briefly degrading operator visibility.
When MCP-server failures aren't obvious from `/mcp`, the recommended next step is `claude --debug`, which logs spawn lines and transport-close events.
A characteristic Claude Code debug log message on MCP transport closure is "Server transport closed unexpectedly, this is likely due to the process exiting early."
claims.notes: F2.3; observed behavior, not stable contract.

claims.text: `MCP_TIMEOUT` (env var) controls MCP server startup timeout in Claude Code.
A per-server `"timeout": <milliseconds>` field in `.mcp.json` sets a hard wall-clock cap on each tool call.
The Claude Code HTTP first-byte budget has a 60-second minimum regardless of configuration, and below-1000 timeout values floor at one second.
Stdio MCP servers must direct all log output to stderr; logging to stdout corrupts the JSON-RPC framing on the transport.
claims.notes: F3.1; cites Anthropic MCP Debugging docs.

claims.text: The MCP host application captures stdio servers' stderr automatically.
Orchestrators must consume stdio MCP servers' stderr continuously or the stdio process can block when the buffer fills.
For transports beyond stdio (notably HTTP), the spec-canonical log channel is the `notifications/message` JSON-RPC notification.
MCP `notifications/message` carries a `level` field per RFC 5424 (debug, info, notice, warning, error, critical, alert, emergency), an optional `logger` name, and arbitrary JSON `data`.
MCP clients adjust the minimum log level via `logging/setLevel`.
MCP log messages MUST NOT contain credentials or secrets.
Claude Desktop writes per-server logs to `~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp*.log` on macOS and `%APPDATA%\Claude\logs\mcp*.log` on Windows.
Claude Code does not publish canonical per-server MCP log paths equivalent to Claude Desktop's, but practitioners adopt the same per-server-file convention.
There is no MCP-canonical log rotation policy; operators apply standard log-rotation tooling.
In Codespaces / devcontainer use, log files inside the container survive container restarts only if on a persisted volume; ephemeral container deletion loses logs unless exported.
Industry practice (multiple vendor MCP-logging guides converge) is structured JSON on stderr with request ID, server name, method, and timestamp.
Synchronous MCP logging is discouraged; practitioners should use async (non-blocking) loggers.
Debug-level MCP logging should be disabled in production.
No single canonical schema for the JSON structure of MCP structured log records exists.
The MCP logging spec SHOULD rate-limit, validate, and monitor for sensitive content in log messages.
The MCP spec is normative on the prohibition of credentials in logs but silent on the technique for enforcement.

The most reliable redaction pattern documented in production MCP write-ups is to overwrite known-sensitive header names and env-var names with `[REDACTED]` at the instrumentation layer before the trace/log record is exported.
Targeting credential redaction by known name (e.g., `Authorization`, `X-Api-Key`, `Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key`) is more reliable than regex pattern-matching on credential shapes.

Header-name-targeted redaction misses credentials that appear in URL query strings or in tool-call argument bodies; a defense-in-depth approach combines name-based redaction with shape-based regex as a backstop.
The OWASP MCP Top-10 (2025) ranks Token Mismanagement and Secret Exposure as MCP01 — the highest-priority MCP risk.

OWASP MCP01 recommended controls cluster around ephemeral context for credential-touching operations, protected diagnostic-trace storage with strict access control, and redaction before write to logs/telemetry.
OWASP MCP01 advises to "Redact or mask secrets before writing to logs or telemetry."
Claude Code's `.mcp.json` schema uses `${VAR_NAME}` substitution for credentials and an explicit `env` block for server-process environment variables.
The names of all credential-bearing env vars are knowable at registration time in `.mcp.json`, which makes env-var-name-driven redaction a particularly good fit for this project.
The augmented `auditing-mcp` could enforce a redaction-list-equals-env-vars-list invariant.

Claude Code's operator-visible MCP failure surface is the union of the `/mcp` panel showing `failed` state with manual-retry affordance, `claude mcp list` showing the same state at shell level, and `--debug`-mode stderr lines.
There is no canonical structured "MCP failure record" emitted as a separate event file by Claude Code by default.
Claude Code's session log captures transport events but is not formatted as a structured record per failure; projects that want a structured per-failure record build it themselves.
The dev-container specification (Microsoft) does not include a native health-check field analogous to Docker Compose's `healthcheck` or Kubernetes' readiness probes.
Microsoft's tracking issue #786 (vscode-dev-containers) acknowledges the absence of a dev-container health-check primitive as an open feature request.
The community convention for devcontainer health-assertion is to run scripts in `postStartCommand` (every container start) and one-time validation in `postCreateCommand`.
MCP health-check surfacing inside a Codespace is greenfield because devcontainers lack a native health-check primitive — the project chooses its own pattern.

Coder dev containers surface failure feedback through startup-script log files at known paths (e.g., `/tmp/coder-startup-script.log`), a dashboard/status surface showing per-service running state, and recommended diagnostic commands such as `docker ps`.
The containerized-dev-environment failure-feedback pattern emphasizes the known log file path as the primary recourse and the dashboard as the at-a-glance surface.

Codespaces does not have an equivalent "service dashboard" inside the container; the operator-visible surface is whatever the project assembles (stderr banner, MOTD on attach, dedicated log file, or per-server check in `postStart`).

Across surveyed sources (Anthropic MCP docs, vendor MCP server docs, MCP-monitoring write-ups, devcontainer troubleshooting docs, OWASP MCP Top-10), no consensus pattern exists for how a primary-MCP-to-fallback-MCP transition is surfaced operator-visibly when the fallback fires in-product.

The MCP literature treats MCP servers as independent — a server is either available or failed — and does not address the "primary degraded; using fallback" semantic that ADR-0018 codifies for GitNexus → codebase-memory-mcp.
The closest analogue to MCP primary-to-fallback surfacing is the generic "circuit-breaker open → using fallback path" pattern from microservice literature, but it is not MCP-specific.

Design Option (a) for MCP primary-to-fallback surfacing is a stderr banner on transition (e.g., "[MCP] primary `gitnexus` unhealthy; agent `discovery-codebase-researcher` proceeding on fallback `codebase-memory-mcp`").

Design Option (b) for MCP primary-to-fallback surfacing is a dedicated event file in the project's runtime log surface (e.g., `.claude/runtime/mcp-events.jsonl`) with `event: fallback_exercised, primary, fallback, agent, ts`.
Design Option (c) for MCP primary-to-fallback surfacing is agent-level acknowledgement in the agent's own output — the sub-agent that triggers the fallback names it explicitly in its result.
Option (b) (dedicated structured event file) aligns most cleanly with the existing audit + structured-record discipline this project already practices for state transitions.
Option (a) (stderr banner) is lowest-friction for surfacing MCP fallback transitions but is ephemeral.
Option (c) (agent-level acknowledgement) places the obligation on each consuming agent, which has uniformity risk.

For small MCP deployments (≤10 concurrent users, ≤50 tools), the recommended monitoring path is to start with local structured logs to per-server files, add structured log forwarding only when the team grows, then add dashboards/alerting last.
Prometheus/Grafana is overkill for single-operator local Codespace MCP use; OpenTelemetry can be added later without redesigning the local surface.
SigNoz's monitoring recommendation is shaped by their commercial interest, but the underlying "start local, add telemetry later" advice is consistent across multiple sources.

For runtime monitoring without a remote telemetry sink, the documented pattern is an active ping-loop — a small supervisor process that issues `ping` to each registered MCP server on a 30-second interval, logs the result, and surfaces three consecutive failures as a state change.

An active ping-loop adds a moving part (the supervisor) that itself needs to be supervised; for a seven-server Codespace, the supervisor can be a `postStart` script that runs once at attach time rather than a long-running daemon.

ToolHive and similar proxy patterns decouple MCP observability from the server itself — the supervisor sits in front of the server's stdio transport and captures messages without requiring server-side code changes.
The proxy/supervisor observability pattern is useful when the operator does not control the upstream MCP server (e.g., GitNexus, Serena, Terraform MCP — none of which this project authors).
ToolHive itself is heavier than what this project needs; the transferable conceptual takeaway is to instrument at the transport layer, not inside the server.
Liveness probing for MCP is solved at the protocol level via the `ping` primitive, which works across stdio and HTTP transports.
A one-shot ping-each-server health check at `postStart` is the lowest-overhead implementation for a seven-server Codespace that aligns with both the MCP protocol and the devcontainer lifecycle.

The FR-9 structured-failure-record is the project's augmentation to Claude Code's baseline transport-event surface — Claude Code does not emit a structured per-failure record by default, so the project building one is a genuine value-add, not a duplication.
The project's runtime log redactor should consume the `env` block of `.mcp.json` as its allowlist of names-to-redact rather than relying on regex shape-matching.
The recommended convention is per-server structured JSON logs on stderr, written to `~/.claude/runtime/<server>.log` or equivalent.
Log-rotation is operator-owned and not specified by any MCP source; `logrotate` or a date-stamped file convention both work.
MCP primary-to-fallback transition surfacing is greenfield — nothing in the surveyed literature gives Design a pattern to copy.

Open question OQ-A: there is no external source dictating the right log-path convention inside the Codespace (`.claude/runtime/<server>.log`, `/tmp/mcp-<server>.log`, or `$XDG_STATE_HOME/claude/mcp/<server>.log`); the `KB-mcp-platform` skill should codify a default once `design-codespaces` proposes one.

Open question OQ-B: whether the augmented `auditing-mcp` should enforce "redaction-list ⊇ `.mcp.json` env-vars-list" as a BLOCKER rule is a Design choice informed by F4.4 but not externally precedented.

Open question OQ-C: for the primary-to-fallback transition, this research note recommends Option (b) (structured event file) but Design owns the final choice; forwards as a Design question to `design-cc` under UI-11 and to `design-composer` for cross-cutting consistency.

Open question OQ-D: it is unknown whether Codespaces or Claude Code exposes a canonical "container is attaching" event hook beyond `postAttachCommand`; no source surveyed addressed this directly and resolution may require codebase-research or experimentation.
